sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

Create an animated, non-interactive surfing pelican using html/3js

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.

arguments.content: Pelican · afternoon glass

# Surfing Pelican

An animated, non-interactive 3D scene: a stylized pelican carving across a
GPU-displaced ocean at golden hour. Built with [three.js](https://threejs.org/)
and bundled as a single self-contained page.

## Running

Serve this folder with any static server and open `index.html`:

```bash
npx serve .
```

The page runs entirely offline — no network requests and no storage.

## What is in the scene

- **Ocean** — a 400×400 plane displaced in the vertex shader by a sum of four
  sine waves. The same wave definitions (`waves.js`) drive both the GPU
  displacement and the CPU buoyancy, so the surfer rides exactly on the
  visible surface. Normals are recomputed analytically for correct lighting.
- **Pelican** — modelled procedurally from three.js primitives: an ellipsoid
  body, a tube neck, a head with a long orange mandible and a wobbling throat
  pouch, flapping extruded wings, webbed feet and a tail fan.
- **Surfboard** — a bevelled extruded outline with a stripe and fin. The whole
  surfer group is oriented to the wave normal and banked into the turn.
- **Water spray** — a recycled pool of soft point particles thrown from the
  board's tail.
- **Sky** — a gradient dome with a sun glow shader and drifting cloud clusters,
  plus a foam disc on the water and a cinematic follow camera.

## Files

| File        | Purpose                                        |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `index.html`| Entry point and page chrome                    |
| `main.js`   | Scene assembly, surfer path and render loop    |
| `waves.js`  | Shared wave model (CPU + generated GLSL)       |
| `ocean.js`  | Displaced water mesh                           |
| `pelican.js`| Procedural pelican and surfboard               |
| `sky.js`    | Sky dome, sun glow and clouds                  |
| `spray.js`  | Particle spray system                          |

## Build check

```bash
esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null
```

content.text:
Built an animated, non-interactive surfing pelican scene in the current directory.

**What it does**
- A stylized pelican procedurally modelled from three.js primitives (ellipsoid body, tube neck, head with long orange mandible + wobbling throat pouch, flapping extruded wings, webbed feet, tail fan) rides a surfboard around a large carving circle.
- The surfer is oriented to the actual wave surface normal and banked into the turn, with wing flap, body bob, head sway and a pulsing pouch.
- The ocean is a 400×400 plane displaced on the GPU by four summed sine waves; normals are recomputed analytically for lighting. The exact same wave model runs on the CPU, so the pelican always sits on the visible surface.
- Recycled soft-point water spray fires from the board's tail, a procedural canvas foam disc slides on the surface, and a gradient sky dome with sun glow plus drifting clouds completes the scene. A cinematic follow camera smooths behind the surfer.

**Files created**
- `index.html` — entry point (loads `main.js` as a module, inline CSS)
- `main.js` — renderer, lights, path, camera and loop
- `waves.js` — shared wave model + generated GLSL
- `ocean.js` — GPU-displaced water
- `pelican.js` — procedural pelican and surfboard
- `sky.js` — sky dome, sun glow, clouds
- `spray.js` — particle spray
- `README.md`

All assets are generated in code (no URLs/storage), and `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` succeeds.
